title: Job Aids for People Managers & Contract Leads
content: Job Aids for People Managers & Contract Leads These job aids provide practical tools for managing the people and delivery situations that arise on Focus teams. They are intended to help People Managers and Contract Leads respond consistently, distinguish individual concerns from delivery-system problems, and intervene at the appropriate level. Job Aids - Job Aid 01: Coaching vs. Performance vs. Systemic Issues — Determine what is preventing a team member from meeting expectations and respond with coaching, performance management, or changes to the delivery system. - Job Aid 02: Giving Effective Feedback — For managers, leads, and all team members: give timely, specific feedback to one another and follow through on agreed actions using principles from Scaling People and Crucial Conversations. - Job Aid 03: Conducting Exit Interviews — Use a 30-minute interview guide, optional prompts, and copyable notes and action templates to learn from departures and improve the experience for future team members.

title: Job Aid 01: Coaching vs. Performance vs. Systemic Issues
content: Job Aid 01: Coaching vs. Performance vs. Systemic Issues When a team member is struggling, the first question should not be “Is this a performance problem?” The first question is: What is preventing this person from consistently meeting the expectation? A missed commitment, communication breakdown, quality concern, or lack of ownership can have very different root causes. Before escalating an issue, determine whether you are dealing with a coaching issue, performance issue, or systemic issue . The Three Categories Category What it means Manager's responsibility --- --- --- Coaching Issue The person needs additional skill, clarity, feedback, experience, or support to consistently meet the expectation. Teach, clarify, demonstrate, provide feedback, and create opportunities to practice. Performance Issue The expectation is reasonable and understood, the person has the capability and support to meet it, but the gap continues despite feedback and coaching. Establish accountability, document the recurring gap, set explicit improvement expectations, and follow Focus's performance-management process when appropriate. Systemic Issue The environment, process, workload, dependencies, leadership decisions, or team structure are preventing reliable performance. Fix the system rather than treating the individual as the problem. The Diagnostic When you observe a delivery concern, work through these questions before categorizing it as a performance issue : Ask If NO... If YES... --- --- --- 1. Is the expectation clear and appropriate for this person's role and level? Clarify the expectation. Continue. 2. Is the person reasonably in control of the outcome? Investigate dependencies/system constraints. Continue. 3. Does the person have the knowledge and skill to meet the expectation? Coach/develop. Continue. 4. Has the person received specific feedback about the gap? Give feedback. Continue. 5. Have reasonable support, resources, and time been provided? Provide support. Continue. 6. Does the same gap continue after expectations, feedback, and support are clear? Continue coaching/observation. This may now be a performance issue . A useful shorthand is: CAN'T → Coaching The person does not yet have the skill, experience, clarity, or judgment needed to consistently meet the expectation. WON'T / ISN'T → Performance The person understands the expectation, has the capability and reasonable support to meet it, has received feedback, and the behavior or outcome continues. CAN'T BECAUSE → Systemic Something in the team's environment is preventing success. Evidence Before Labels Retro comments, stakeholder feedback, missed sprint commitments, defects, escalations, or concerns raised by another lead should be treated as signals , not conclusions. Before having a performance conversation, the manager should be able to answer: 1. What specifically happened? 2. What was expected instead? 3. Was that expectation previously clear? 4. What impact did the gap have? 5. What feedback or coaching has already been provided? 6. Has the behavior occurred repeatedly? Avoid labels such as: “You aren't taking ownership.” Instead, describe observable behavior and the expected behavior: “On the last two deliverables, I had to follow up several times to understand status and next steps. At your level, I expect you to proactively communicate progress, surface blockers, and close the loop without repeated prompting.” Specific behavior can be coached. Vague character judgments cannot. Common Scenarios Scenario Start Here What to investigate --- --- --- Team member requires repeated follow-ups Coaching Do they understand expectations for follow-through, prioritization, and closing loops? Progress isn't visible to the team or lead Coaching / Systemic Is work actually stalled, or is progress simply not being communicated? Senior team member isn't demonstrating expected ownership Coaching / Role Clarity Have ownership expectations for their level been explicitly established? Decisions are difficult to understand or poorly explained Coaching Can they clearly communicate the recommendation, rationale, tradeoffs, and next action? Team member repeatedly surfaces problems without helping move them forward Coaching Do they know when they are expected to recommend an action, facilitate resolution, or escalate? Team member reports that work is on track, declines support, then repeatedly misses commitments Potential Performance Issue Were risks knowable, expectations clear, and support available? Is this recurring after feedback? Several team members are struggling with the same issue Systemic Look at workload, priorities, dependencies, process, leadership, tooling, and role clarity. Individual has too many competing priorities Systemic first Who established the priorities? What should be stopped or deprioritized? Team receives conflicting direction from leaders Systemic Leadership must align priorities and decision rights before evaluating individual execution. Team member struggles with a new responsibility they've never performed before Coaching Determine what training, modeling, pairing, or feedback they need. A Missed Commitment Is Not Automatically a Performance Issue In delivery environments, commitments move. Requirements change. Dependencies fail. Stakeholders introduce new priorities. Technical complexity emerges. The manager should therefore investigate how the individual managed the commitment , not merely whether the date was missed. There is a meaningful difference between: “We're at risk of missing Friday because the dependency hasn't been resolved. I've escalated it, and here are our options.” and: “Everything is fine.” followed by an unexpected miss. The second situation may indicate a reliability or judgment concern because the team lost the opportunity to manage the risk. Expectations for Senior Team Members and Leads As responsibility increases, Focus expects greater independence in creating clarity and moving work forward. Senior team members should increasingly be able to: - Own the outcome , not simply complete assigned tasks. - Surface risk early , while the team still has options. - Close the loop without repeated prompting. - Make thinking visible by clearly explaining decisions and tradeoffs. - Move problems forward , even when they do not personally know the solution. - Protect team focus by identifying competing priorities and escalating capacity constraints. This does not mean leaders must always arrive with a solution. A healthy escalation can be: “I don't know the solution yet. Here's what I think is happening, here's what I've tried, and here's where I need help.” The expectation is not “Never bring me a problem.” The expectation is “Help move the problem forward.” Moving From Coaching to Performance Management A coaching issue should not remain in an informal coaching loop indefinitely. Consider transitioning into formal performance management when: Expectation is clear → Capability exists → Feedback has been given → Support has been provided → Reasonable time has passed → The same material gap continues At that point, the conversation changes from: Coaching: “Let's work on helping you become more effective at this.” to: Performance: “This is an expectation of your role, we've discussed the gap and provided support, and the required improvement has not occurred consistently.” People Managers should involve the appropriate Focus leadership/People Operations before beginning formal performance action. Scrum Metrics Are Signals, Not Individual Scorecards Do not use velocity, story points completed, ticket counts, PR counts, bugs, or similar Scrum metrics as standalone measures of individual performance. They can help identify where investigation is needed, but they rarely explain why something is happening. Evaluate people more holistically through: Reliability • Quality • Ownership • Collaboration • Judgment • Communication • Role Competency • Impact The goal is not to create a delivery organization where everyone learns how to make their metrics look green. The goal is to create teams where problems become visible early enough to solve them.

title: Job Aid 02: Giving Effective Feedback
content: Job Aid 02: Giving Effective Feedback Why feedback matters and how managers, leads, and teammates can give useful feedback to one another. Feedback gives people information they need to succeed: what is working, what needs to change, and how their actions affect others. When a concern stays unspoken or circulates among colleagues, the person involved has little opportunity to understand it or respond. Feedback flows in every direction: between teammates, from leads to team members, and from team members to leads and managers. You do not need a management title or reporting relationship to share an observation, explain its impact, or ask for a change in how you work together. This job aid applies principles from Claire Hughes Johnson's Scaling People and Crucial Conversations to Focus delivery situations. The examples and suggested cadence below are practical applications for our teams. Why Giving Feedback Is Part of Working Together Each of us sees effects of the work that others may miss: the downstream effect of a late handoff, the uncertainty created by a missing update, or the value of a well-timed escalation. Sharing those observations helps people connect their work to team outcomes, regardless of role or seniority. - Make expectations visible. Refer to shared agreements and explain what you need to work well together. Managers and leads should also clarify expectations for a person's role and level. If an expectation has not been discussed, establish it together or involve the person responsible for setting it. - Give people time to adjust. Raise concerns while the details are fresh and there is an opportunity to practice a different approach. Waiting for a review or the next retro can allow the same issue to repeat. - Reinforce what works. Specific positive feedback tells people which behaviors to repeat and helps the team learn from good delivery practices. - Improve shared understanding. Either person may learn about unclear priorities, missing support, or a decision that needs to be revisited. A concern discussed with others still needs an appropriate conversation with the person involved. Talking about someone does not give them feedback. This supports Focus's existing approach of active coaching and clear expectations. Everyone can give feedback; formal performance assessment and corrective action remain with the responsible managers and appropriate Focus leadership/People Operations. Job Aid 01 helps managers and leads distinguish coaching, performance, and systemic concerns as they learn more. Principles from Scaling People Hughes Johnson emphasizes managerial self-awareness, curiosity when coaching, and the willingness to surface difficult topics. She describes feedback as a partnership in which the manager offers observations and explores what is happening, rather than assuming they already have the answer. See her discussion of these principles. Although Hughes Johnson discusses these principles in a management context, the same curiosity and self-awareness are useful in peer feedback and feedback to a lead or manager. Apply that approach by: - Checking your own contribution. Was the shared agreement clear? Did your own actions or requests contribute to the problem? Are you reacting to a work-style preference or a meaningful delivery gap? - Bringing an observation and a question. Be specific about what you saw, then investigate the explanation together. - Naming the concern respectfully. If a recurring issue matters to the work or relationship, make it discussable. Avoid hints that require the other person to guess what you mean. Prepare for a Crucial Conversation Start with Heart: Identify the outcome you want for the person, the team, and your working relationship. Check whether frustration has shifted your goal toward winning an argument or proving someone wrong. Explain your constructive purpose when you open the conversation. Crucial Learning: Start with Heart. Make It Safe: Show respect for the person and concern for shared goals. If the conversation becomes defensive or shuts down, pause to understand what feels threatening and clarify your intent. Give them room to disagree and correct your interpretation while keeping the expectation clear. Crucial Learning: Make It Safe. For sensitive individual feedback, choose a private conversation with enough time to listen. Prepare one or two concrete examples and the impact you can substantiate. Distinguish what you observed directly from what someone else reported, and avoid presenting secondhand concerns as established facts. Use STATE to Open the Dialogue The STATE framework helps you explain your perspective and invite the other person's. The last two skills describe how to speak throughout the conversation. Crucial Learning's explanation of STATE. Skill How to apply it --- --- Share your facts Describe a specific event or behavior that could be observed. Avoid labels such as “unreliable” or “not committed.” Tell your story Explain the concern or interpretation the facts raise for you. Distinguish an actual impact from a risk you anticipate. Ask for others' paths Invite their account of what happened. Listen before choosing a response. Talk tentatively Treat your explanation of the cause as something to examine. You can be certain about an agreed expectation while remaining curious about why it was missed. Encourage testing Explicitly welcome corrections, missing context, and a different interpretation. Change your view when the evidence warrants it. Example: Repeated Follow-Ups “I'd like us to make handoffs easier to plan. On the last two deliverables, the agreed status update wasn't posted, and I asked twice before learning the next steps. That left me unable to confirm the handoff with the team. I'm concerned our current approach isn't making progress and blockers visible enough. What was happening from your perspective? Is there context I'm missing?” Pause and listen. If the update expectation was unclear, clarify the agreement together. If competing assignments prevented progress, involve the lead who can resolve the priorities. If an agreed update was missed, discuss what would make the handoff work more reliably. Then agree on a concrete next step, for example: “Could we both post progress, the next step, and any blocker in the agreed channel before our check-in for the next two weeks? I'll ask our lead to clarify which assignment takes priority today. Let's check together next week to see whether handoffs are clearer.” Example: Feedback to a Lead or Manager “In the last two planning meetings, a new priority was added without identifying what should move out. I left unsure which commitment to keep, and work on the original priority stalled. Could we make the tradeoff explicit when priorities change? Is there context about those decisions that would help me understand them?” If you are receiving feedback from someone you lead, listen, acknowledge the impact, and explain what you will change or clarify. Your response helps determine whether they will feel able to raise the next concern. Example: Reinforcing Good Practice “You flagged the dependency risk before planning and brought two options. That gave us time to adjust the commitment with the client. Please keep surfacing risks that early; it helps the team make decisions while we still have options.” Common Scenarios Situation Useful response --- --- A concern appears in a retro Use the retro to understand the team pattern. Follow up privately on individual behavior; do not turn the group discussion into an individual performance review. You are waiting for the person to notice the problem State the observation, impact, and expectation directly. Seniority does not make unspoken expectations clear. The person disagrees or becomes upset Listen for missing facts or a misunderstanding. A reaction alone does not establish a performance issue. If needed, agree on a short pause and a specific time to resume. The same gap continues after feedback Revisit the agreement and what remains unresolved. If you cannot resolve it together, bring concrete examples and the steps already tried to the appropriate lead or People Manager. Managers and leads can use Job Aid 01 to assess the concern; formal performance action requires the appropriate Focus leadership/People Operations involvement. Someone gives you difficult feedback Ask for an example, check your understanding, and explain what you will do with the input. Follow up on your own commitments. For issues covered by Focus's Conduct & Ethics or Incident Response procedures, use the applicable reporting path; this job aid does not add a requirement to confront someone first. End with Action and Follow Through Crucial Conversations emphasizes turning dialogue into specific commitments: identify an owner, the action, a deadline, and a follow-up. A conversation can feel productive while leaving those decisions unresolved. Al Switzler on moving to action. Before closing, confirm: - The behavior to continue or change and what success will look like. - The support or changes each person can provide, and anything that needs a lead's or manager's decision. - Who is responsible for each action and when it will happen. - When you will review progress together. When a recap would help, confirm the agreement privately with the other person, including both perspectives and each person's commitments. Managers should use the appropriate management record when formal documentation is needed. Recognize improvement at follow-up and address any remaining gap explicitly. Suggested Practice Before the Next Retro Use the next 30 days as a learning window, adjusting timing to the situation: 1. Early in the window: Choose one meaningful concern, gather examples, and have the conversation. Also identify a helpful behavior to reinforce. 2. During the window: Check progress at an agreed check-in with the other person. Complete your own commitments and adjust the approach if new information changes your understanding. 3. At the next retro: Discuss team-level actions, what changed, and what remains blocked. Keep individual feedback and personnel details in the appropriate private conversations. The next retro is a checkpoint. Give feedback when it can help, rather than saving it for that meeting.

title: Job Aid 03: Conducting Exit Interviews
content: Job Aid 03: Conducting Exit Interviews A reusable interview guide and notes template for learning from a departing team member's experience at Focus. An exit interview helps Focus understand what supported someone’s success, what made their work harder, and what influenced their decision to leave. Use the conversation to identify practices worth preserving and improvements in management, onboarding, team relationships, and delivery operations. This guide works across roles, practices, and client engagements. Plan for 30 minutes , with up to 45 minutes if the departing person wants more time. Ask the core questions first and use the optional prompts selectively. For a planned contract end or other departure the person did not choose, adapt the departure questions to their experience of the transition. Jump to the 30-minute interview, optional prompts, notes template, or action tracker. Before the Interview - Choose an interviewer who can receive candid feedback. Where possible, offer someone outside the direct reporting relationship. If the feedback concerns the interviewer, offer another appropriate Focus leader or People Operations contact. - Explain the purpose in advance. Invite participation, allow the person to skip questions, and offer written feedback or a shorter follow-up if they prefer. Keep equipment return, final administrative tasks, and handover logistics in a separate conversation. - Confirm how feedback will be handled. Identify who needs access to the notes and who will receive a summary. Do not promise complete confidentiality or anonymity. Explain that some concerns may need to be shared with the people responsible for addressing them. - Prepare without forming a verdict. Review the role and dates, then separate what you know from assumptions about the departure. Do not bring a list of accusations for the person to confirm. - Use a private place for notes. Confirm the appropriate restricted location with People Operations. This handbook contains the blank template only; completed notes, recordings, transcripts, and identifying examples belong outside the public handbook and its repository. If recording or using transcription, explain the tool and intended access and obtain explicit agreement before starting. Opening Script Allow about two minutes. Replace the bracketed text with the actual sharing arrangements before the conversation. > “Thank you for taking the time to talk. I want to understand your experience at Focus, what we should keep doing, and what we should improve. You can skip any question or choose to share feedback in writing. > > “I’ll take notes so I can represent your feedback accurately. The notes will be available to [people or roles who need access], and I plan to share [type of summary] with [recipients]. I can’t promise complete confidentiality: if you raise something that needs attention, I may need to involve the appropriate people. I’ll explain the next steps as clearly as I can. > > “I’m here to listen and understand. Before we start, is there anything you would like to know about how this conversation or your feedback will be handled?” The 30 Minute Interview The timings include the opening and total 30 minutes. Ask each numbered question, then choose a follow-up where it will clarify something important. Protect the final nine minutes for the departure decision and closing. If an earlier issue needs more time, offer a follow-up rather than silently dropping those topics. 1. Overall Experience · 3 Minutes How would you describe your experience at Focus overall? Possible follow-ups: - What are you most proud of, or what did you enjoy most? - What was most disappointing or harder than it needed to be? Capture both strengths and difficulties. Let the person choose their own words before suggesting descriptions of the culture. 2. Joining Focus and Understanding the Role · 4 Minutes How did the role and your day-to-day work compare with what you expected when you joined? Possible follow-ups: - What helped you get started, and what was missing from onboarding? - How clear were success expectations for you and for the team? - When did you feel part of the team? What helped or delayed that? Distinguish understanding an individual assignment from understanding the team’s goals, priorities, and definition of success. 3. Manager and Leadership Support · 4 Minutes What was it like working with your manager, and where did you need more support? Possible follow-ups: - What did your manager do that helped you succeed? - What feedback, coaching, or conversation would have helped but did not happen? - What could Focus leadership, including me, have done differently? If the person had both a People Manager and a day-to-day lead, distinguish those relationships. Positive feedback about one kind of support does not answer every question about management or development. 4. Team Relationships and Delivery · 4 Minutes How did the team work together, and where did collaboration become difficult? Possible follow-ups: - Can you describe one decision or handoff that worked well or broke down? - How clear was who could decide, who needed to contribute, and how priorities changed? - How did working relationships affect your ability to do good work? Ask about relevant roles and disciplines without assuming a particular team structure. If a specific relationship matters, ask: “What was it like working with [person]? What worked, and what was difficult?” 5. Speaking Up and Respect · 4 Minutes How comfortable did you feel disagreeing, asking for help, or raising a concern? Possible follow-ups: - Can you share an example of how people responded? - Were there times you decided not to raise something? What influenced that decision? - How were mistakes handled, and did you feel treated with respect? Feeling respected, feeling supported, and feeling safe to disagree are related but distinct. Do not infer that all three were present from an answer about only one. 6. Decision to Leave · 5 Minutes What factors influenced your decision to leave, and when did you begin considering it? Possible follow-ups: - Was there a turning point, or did the decision develop over time? - What mattered most in choosing your next step? - Was there anything Focus could realistically have changed that might have influenced your decision? Allow for several reasons, including positive opportunities elsewhere. Do not assume an improvement suggestion is a reason for leaving unless the person makes that connection. If the departure was not their choice, ask instead: “How have you experienced this transition, and what could Focus have handled better?” 7. Advice and Closing · 4 Minutes What should Focus preserve or change for the next person in a similar role? Then ask: “Is there anything I haven’t asked that you want leadership to understand?” Briefly reflect the main points back: “I heard [strength], [concern], and [suggested change]. What have I missed or misunderstood?” Confirm any agreed follow-up and thank the person. Do not promise an outcome you cannot deliver. Optional Prompts for a Longer Interview Use the extra time to clarify the most relevant topics. This is a question bank, not an additional checklist to finish. Topic Prompts --- --- Role and use of skills Were you able to use your strengths? What work did you expect to do but rarely had time or opportunity to do? Development and feedback What helped you grow? What feedback or practice would have helped you improve? How clear were future opportunities? Onboarding and access What was easy or difficult about equipment, access, documentation, introductions, and learning the client context? Workload and flexibility How manageable were the workload and competing priorities? How did working hours, flexibility, and time away work in practice? Compensation and benefits Did compensation, benefits, or progression influence your experience or decision? What would you like leadership to understand? Connection to Focus How connected did you feel to Focus beyond your immediate project? What helped you learn from people elsewhere in the company? Client and contract environment How did client expectations, approvals, dependencies, or staffing arrangements affect the work? What was within Focus’s control to improve? Cross-functional work How did information move between disciplines? Where did another perspective or a clearer handoff change the result? Specific working relationships What worked well with this person? What was difficult? What happened, and how did it affect you or the work? How to Listen and Follow Up Aim to spend most of the conversation listening. After a useful response, ask one neutral follow-up: “Can you give me an example?” , “What effect did that have?” , or “What would have helped?” Allow a pause before moving on. - Reflect before explaining. Check your understanding of the person’s experience. Save proposed solutions and explanations of leadership decisions for after you have heard the full account. - Avoid leading questions. Replace “Was your manager unsupportive?” with “Where did you need more support?” Replace “Did the team’s conflict make you leave?” with “What factors influenced your decision?” - Separate accounts. Record what the person experienced, what they observed in others, and your own interpretation distinctly. An interviewer’s explanation or a brief “yes” to it is not the same as an independently described experience. - Respect what remains unknown. Mark questions as answered, partially answered, not asked, or declined. Do not fill gaps with assumptions or treat a declined answer as confirmation of a concern. - Respond appropriately to serious concerns. If the person raises conduct, safety, security, or other reportable concerns, explain and follow the applicable Conduct & Ethics or Incident Response path. Do not wait for a routine interview summary or require them to confront the person involved first. Copyable Interview Notes Template Copy this blank structure into the appropriate private record before the interview. Use paraphrases unless you can verify exact wording; label direct quotations clearly. Keep identifiable personnel details in the appropriate restricted record. Removing a name may not make a story anonymous, especially on a small team. Summarize: 1. What worked: practices and support worth preserving. 2. What made work harder: concrete examples and their reported impact. 3. Departure factors: only the reasons the person actually stated; identify what remains unknown. 4. Assessment: possible individual, management, or delivery-system issues and what needs further checking. One interview can justify a practical improvement without proving a company-wide pattern or an individual conduct finding. 5. Actions: a small number of concrete changes with an accountable owner, target date, and a way to check whether the change helped. Use Job Aid 01 when distinguishing coaching, performance, and systemic concerns. Use Job Aid 02 when preparing an appropriate feedback conversation. Serious concerns continue through the existing reporting process. Copyable Action Tracker Copy the blank tracker into the private working record and add one row per accepted action. Suggested owners are roles to assign, not automatic commitments. Route urgent concerns when raised, without waiting for this step. - Within two weeks: review the summary with the appropriate leadership or People Operations contacts and assign owners and dates to accepted actions. Distinguish proposed changes from decisions already made. - At 30 and 60 days: check whether actions changed the experience or the work. Ask current team members or new hires for concrete examples; completed meetings and updated documents alone do not establish improvement. Use these as planning targets, adapting to the situation and any applicable process. When sharing team-level improvements, explain what is changing without exposing private interview details.
